records.hook: The valley that witnessed cultural exchange — Afghanistan. Afghanistan’s Bamiyan Valley sits among the mountains of the central highlands.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: Afghanistan’s Bamiyan Valley sits among the mountains of the central highlands. Over many centuries, Buddhist monastic communities developed cliff sanctuaries and striking works of art here, drawing from different artistic traditions moving across Central and South Asia. The landscape tells a story of connection rather than isolation. Its caves and remaining paintings are evidence of a rich religious and commercial world.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The site is also marked by loss: two monumental Buddha statues were destroyed in 2001. UNESCO regards the empty niches and surviving archaeology as part of an important historical record. Remembering what was lost matters, but it would be a mistake to see the whole of Afghanistan only through destruction. Conservation continues to involve the material that has survived and the wider landscape around it.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Afghanistan contains varied languages, communities, architecture and highland environments. Bamiyan is a strong introduction to those layers because it resists a single narrative. Buddhist art, later Islamic architecture and surrounding settlements occupy different chapters of one landscape, with each period leaving its own evidence.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: What remains in Bamiyan is not an empty story. The exposed niches, surviving sanctuaries and mountains invite careful questions about how ideas and art once travelled enormous distances. The historical tragedy deserves respect, while the living communities and the broader country deserve attention beyond any one monument.

records.quickFact: The Bamiyan Valley preserves both surviving Buddhist-era sanctuaries and the enormous cliff niches from which monumental statues were destroyed.

records.hook: A grassland that held imperial capitals — Mongolia. Mongolia’s Orkhon Valley has been inhabited and travelled through for thousands of years.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: Mongolia’s Orkhon Valley has been inhabited and travelled through for thousands of years. Its grasslands and river formed a landscape that supported changing nomadic communities and large political centres. UNESCO recognises the valley for the way archaeological remains, herding traditions and imperial history fit together rather than existing as separate stories.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The site includes remains associated with successive Central Asian states and with Kharkhorum, a capital of the Mongol Empire. The valleys also hold memorials and religious buildings that reveal changing beliefs over time. It is tempting to imagine empire only as an army on horseback, but the remains here show that administration, trade, religion and settlement also mattered.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Pastoral life still gives the area much of its character. Seasonal movement and use of the grasslands connect contemporary livelihoods to a long environmental history. That connection is not proof nothing has changed; it shows how a broad landscape can continue to be worked and valued while its older remains are protected.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: A traveller following the river could once have encountered major centres of power amid huge areas of open pasture. This contrast is the fascinating part: seemingly empty space was connected by people, routes and ideas. The valley helps explain why Mongolian history belongs to a much wider Eurasian story.

records.quickFact: The Orkhon Valley includes the remains of Kharkhorum, one of the Mongol Empire’s important capitals, amid a living pastoral landscape.

records.hook: A valley of temples, squares and living faith — Nepal. Nepal’s Kathmandu Valley has an extraordinary concentration of buildings and public spaces that preserve centuries of artistic and religious history.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: Nepal’s Kathmandu Valley has an extraordinary concentration of buildings and public spaces that preserve centuries of artistic and religious history. Its UNESCO property includes historic squares in Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, together with important Buddhist stupas and Hindu temple complexes. A walk across the valley can pass between quite different architectural traditions, each still meaningful to its communities.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The intricate woodwork, metalwork and brick architecture show the skills of local craftspeople. These are not simply backdrops for tourism photographs: many spaces continue to be used for worship, festivals and neighbourhood activities. That makes careful conservation especially demanding, as places must remain useful and respected while their material history is preserved.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: The valley also sits at the edge of a much larger Nepalese landscape, stretching towards some of the world’s highest mountains. City life and mountain ecology are linked through geography, resources and routes. The capital’s historic monuments offer one angle on Nepal, but no single valley can capture the cultural diversity found across its regions.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: Pay attention to the way squares function. Open courtyards, temples and streets are parts of a social space that people have used and transformed through generations. Kathmandu Valley becomes more interesting when architecture is read through everyday activity as well as through dates and famous monuments.

records.quickFact: Kathmandu Valley’s UNESCO property includes seven monument zones, from the historic squares to major Buddhist and Hindu sacred sites.

records.hook: The sacred mountain above a Silk Road city — Kyrgyzstan. Above Osh in Kyrgyzstan rises Sulaiman-Too, a mountain associated with ritual and pilgrimage for many centuries.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: Above Osh in Kyrgyzstan rises Sulaiman-Too, a mountain associated with ritual and pilgrimage for many centuries. UNESCO identifies caves, petroglyphs, pathways and places of worship distributed across its slopes. Its position over the Fergana Valley made it a familiar landmark for travellers moving through major Central Asian routes.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The mountain’s significance developed through different belief traditions. Archaeological remains reflect old sacred practices, while later Islamic sites show how people continued to attach meaning to the landscape. This layering matters: Sulaiman-Too is not frozen in one religious period, and its meaning cannot be reduced to the age of a single structure.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Kyrgyzstan is also known for mountain pastures, lakes and herding traditions across the Tian Shan. The mountain at Osh connects that wider environmental setting with urban and spiritual life. It shows how a landmark can carry both a practical role in navigation and a strong cultural importance that persists after routes and governments change.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: The shape of the mountain and its relationship to the surrounding city are part of the protected heritage. Look for the pathways as well as the rock art: they reveal how generations approached particular sites. A mountain can be an archive of movement and belief rather than only a viewpoint.

records.quickFact: Sulaiman-Too’s slopes include ancient carved imagery and later sacred buildings, illustrating changing beliefs over many centuries.

records.hook: At the knot of Asia’s highest ranges — Tajikistan. Eastern Tajikistan contains the huge mountains of the Pamirs, where several major Asian ranges converge.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: Eastern Tajikistan contains the huge mountains of the Pamirs, where several major Asian ranges converge. UNESCO’s Tajik National Park protects a landscape of high plateaux, exceptionally tall peaks and powerful glaciers. The geography can look almost otherworldly, but it is shaped by enormous geological forces, extreme weather and water moving through valleys over long periods.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The park includes many rivers and lakes, some formed or fed by ice. Wildlife has adapted to high altitude and harsh seasonal changes, with species such as snow leopards and wild mountain sheep using remote habitats. Understanding the place means looking beyond one dramatic summit to the whole network of ice, water and mountain ecosystems.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Tajikistan’s cultural story also follows the valleys and routes running between highlands and settled regions. For generations, mountains have influenced communication, farming and movement. The park is sparsely inhabited, but the wider Pamir region has communities and histories that cannot be described simply as empty wilderness.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: A map gives away one astonishing fact: the Pamirs are not merely a line of peaks but a complex meeting of ranges, plateaux and glacial valleys. That makes the area both physically formidable and scientifically valuable. The scenery earns attention, but so do the processes that shaped it.

records.quickFact: The protected Pamir landscape contains mountains above 7,000 metres and vast ice, river and lake systems.

records.hook: Rice fields shaped into mountainsides — Philippines. In the Philippine Cordilleras, the Ifugao have developed a remarkable cultural landscape of terraced rice fields.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: In the Philippine Cordilleras, the Ifugao have developed a remarkable cultural landscape of terraced rice fields. Rather than treating the hills as obstacles, generations created agricultural structures that trace the mountain contours. UNESCO recognises several terrace clusters, each with its own form, including amphitheatre-like slopes and complex terraced valleys.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The terraces are practical farming systems and places with cultural and spiritual significance. Their maintenance requires knowledge about water, soil and seasonal work, passed between generations. That helps explain why simply photographing them without thinking about the farmers misses the core of their importance. They remain living landscapes that depend on people and continued cultivation.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: The Philippines is an archipelago with very different regional histories, languages and environments. The Cordilleras introduce the mountainous north of Luzon, contrasting with coastal cities and tropical marine places elsewhere. This is a useful reminder that national geography includes far more than the beaches most travel posters emphasise.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: What makes the terraces so compelling is their scale and patience. A field wall seems small, but thousands of connected choices transform an entire mountainside. The achievement is simultaneously engineering, agriculture and cultural tradition, and its future relies on all three continuing to matter. Their continued upkeep is a real achievement by the communities who live and farm here.

records.quickFact: Some Ifugao rice terraces follow whole mountain amphitheatres, turning steep slopes into working fields.

records.hook: A swamp that records the beginnings of farming — Papua New Guinea. The highlands of Papua New Guinea hold the Kuk Early Agricultural Site, an extraordinary record of how people gradually changed wetland environments for growing crops.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: The highlands of Papua New Guinea hold the Kuk Early Agricultural Site, an extraordinary record of how people gradually changed wetland environments for growing crops. UNESCO describes archaeological evidence of drainage channels, cultivation mounds and other land management features developed over thousands of years. It is a place where the most important remains are not a palace or a statue but marks made in the ground.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The site helps researchers trace how cultivation became more organised over long periods. Its buried features show a sophisticated understanding of wet conditions and soil. Archaeology here is therefore a story of experimentation and practical knowledge, not a simple moment when someone invented agriculture. The waterlogged setting has helped preserve evidence that might disappear in drier places.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Papua New Guinea has many languages and communities spread between highlands, forests and coasts. Kuk represents one distinctive chapter in this diversity and reminds us that complex agricultural histories developed in several regions of the world. It also gives present-day landscapes new meaning: ordinary-looking fields may contain records of extremely old decisions.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: Imagine spending generations improving drainage and growing techniques, with each layer leaving traces for archaeologists. Kuk shows how gradual local changes could alter a whole way of life. Its importance lies in long-term human ingenuity, sustained by a wetland environment that both challenged and preserved those efforts.

records.quickFact: Archaeologists at Kuk have identified evidence of wetland agriculture extending back roughly 7,000 years or more.

records.hook: Stonework from an Andean power centre — Bolivia. High on Bolivia’s Altiplano near Lake Titicaca stand the monumental remains of Tiwanaku, a major political and ceremonial centre of the pre-Hispanic Andes.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: High on Bolivia’s Altiplano near Lake Titicaca stand the monumental remains of Tiwanaku, a major political and ceremonial centre of the pre-Hispanic Andes. UNESCO describes a city that reached particular importance during the first millennium CE. Its carefully shaped stone structures and planned ceremonial spaces reveal architectural skill and powerful institutions from centuries before the Inca Empire.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: What survives today is only part of the original city. Much of the wider settlement was made using materials less durable than the monumental stonework, so the standing buildings can distort our view of how people lived. Researchers use excavation and context to understand Tiwanaku’s organisation, influence and long-distance relationships across the highland region.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Bolivia’s landscapes range from this cold plateau to much lower and greener environments. The Tiwanaku ruins help bring the Altiplano into a cultural story rather than treating it as an empty high-altitude backdrop. Its communities built meaning into architecture, ritual and routes connecting different ecological zones.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: The precision of stone fitting often attracts attention, but equally interesting is the scale of planning needed to organise the site. Tiwanaku reminds us how varied the ancient Americas were, with distinct centres of power and artistic traditions that should not be folded into one generic “Inca” story.

records.quickFact: Tiwanaku’s ceremonial centre stands roughly 3,850 metres above sea level, near Lake Titicaca.

records.hook: An old port that breaks the colonial grid — Uruguay. Uruguay’s Colonia del Sacramento began as a Portuguese settlement on the Río de la Plata in 1680.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: Uruguay’s Colonia del Sacramento began as a Portuguese settlement on the Río de la Plata in 1680. Its waterfront position placed it in a zone of rivalry between Portuguese and Spanish interests, and its surviving buildings reflect that contested past. UNESCO notes that the old quarter has a less rigid street plan than many Spanish colonial towns, adapting instead to the peninsula and its military setting.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The city was repeatedly disputed, and different periods contributed to its urban character. Its streets and buildings illustrate a mixture of Portuguese, Spanish and later influences. Walkways, low walls and a river-facing skyline reveal how closely the settlement was tied to both defence and trade across the estuary.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Uruguay has a wider social and cultural life beyond the historic port. Colonia is an appealing way to start because its scale makes urban history visible: the lanes, houses and waterfront can be explored as a coherent place rather than a disconnected collection of monuments. It also provides a counterpoint to the modern capital, Montevideo.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: Look closely at the street pattern. The irregular arrangement, rather than a perfectly ordered checkerboard, reflects the local topography and the circumstances of its founding. That detail turns an attractive old town into a lesson about how politics and geography can shape everyday space.

records.quickFact: Colonia del Sacramento preserves a historic urban plan that differs from the regular grids associated with many Spanish colonial cities.

records.hook: An immense rainforest protecting river origins — Suriname. In the middle of Suriname lies a vast protected area of largely continuous tropical rainforest.

sections.title: A place with a history
sections.body: In the middle of Suriname lies a vast protected area of largely continuous tropical rainforest. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve safeguards upper river watersheds and a range of lowland and mountainous forest habitats. UNESCO describes its remarkable plant diversity and the importance of conserving such an extensive tropical ecosystem in one connected area.

sections.title: The landscapes around it
sections.body: The forest supports a wide range of animals, including large mammals and colourful birds. Its ecological importance depends on connections among rivers, canopy habitats, geology and climate rather than any single iconic species. Protecting the headwaters helps preserve processes that extend well beyond the reserve boundaries.

sections.title: The people behind the place
sections.body: Suriname’s cultural identity also includes diverse communities and histories shaped by rivers, forests and Atlantic connections. A rainforest should not be treated as a blank green space on a map. Its environmental significance is real, but so too are the people and knowledge associated with the broader landscape.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body: One reason the reserve stands out is the scale on which natural systems remain linked. A river beginning deep in the forest can connect the uplands to distant settlements and coasts. The atlas should help readers imagine those connections instead of reducing the country to a photograph of trees. Its scale also explains why protecting an intact forest can matter to distant waterways and wildlife.

records.quickFact: Central Suriname Nature Reserve protects around 1.6 million hectares of tropical forest, including several major river headwaters.
